summary: Children model shapes two ways: BUILDING them from components (sticks or straws as edges, clay balls or connectors as vertices) and DRAWING them. This procedural work turns attribute knowledge into action — knowing a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners means reaching for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joining them into a CLOSED loop; building a cube means coordinating 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces into a genuine 3-D frame rather than a flat square. It is the 'doing' counterpart of describing and analysing shapes, and it exposes whether a child truly holds a shape's structure. Teach by naming the attributes and counting the parts before building, insisting on closure, and supporting straight drawn sides with grids or a straight edge.
misconceptions: Uses the wrong number of components — grabs 4 sticks for a triangle, or the wrong count of straws/connectors for a cube — not matching parts to the shape's attributes.
Leaves the figure OPEN or makes wobbly/curved sides, so the corners don't join into a closed shape.
Builds a cube flat as a single square or a laid-out cross, not raising it into a closed 3-D frame.
Draws only the prototypical wide, horizontal rectangle (or rounds the corners) and cannot draw a tall or tilted one.

activities.title: Build a triangle from counted components
steps: Name the attributes aloud first: 'a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners, so I need 3 sticks and 3 balls.'
Count out exactly 3 sticks and 3 clay balls before joining anything.
Join the sticks at the balls into a CLOSED loop so every corner meets.
Check the finished model against a real triangle.
Then make a different triangle — a long thin one — so the build is driven by the attributes, not one remembered picture.
activities.insight: A shape's attributes tell you which parts to gather and how to join them; a triangle must be a closed figure of 3 straight sides meeting at 3 corners, and many different triangles satisfy that.

activities.title: Draw a rectangle (and a non-canonical one)
steps: Draw a recognisable rectangle on dotted paper or a geoboard, marking each side as it is made.
Use a straight edge to keep each of the four sides straight and join the four corners so the figure is closed.
Then make a tall rectangle (longer than it is wide) or a tilted one, not only the wide horizontal version.
activities.insight: A rectangle is a closed figure with four straight sides and four square (not rounded) corners; a tall or tilted rectangle is just as valid as the familiar wide one.

activities.title: Build a cube frame: from one square to a solid
steps: Using sticks that are all the same length, build one square face first from 4 sticks and 4 balls.
Raise 4 vertical sticks from the corners of that square (adding 4 more balls at their tops).
Cap them with a second square on top, so the flat face lifts into a solid frame.
Count the finished frame: 12 edges (sticks), 8 vertices (balls) and the 6 square faces — in a skeleton frame these are the six square openings the edges enclose.
Compare against a real cube and check the counts match.
activities.insight: A cube is more than a single square: it is a 3-D frame of 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, built by raising one face to a second.

checkQuestion: Set three tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Use these sticks and balls to make a triangle.' (2) 'Draw a rectangle.' (3) 'Now build a cube with these straws and connectors.'
checkAnswer: (1) A closed triangle — 3 sticks joined at 3 balls. (2) A recognisable rectangle — a closed figure with four roughly-straight sides and four corners (longer than wide is fine). (3) A cube frame of 12 straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices) forming 6 square faces. The child selects the right number of parts and closes the shape, using its attributes to guide the build.
